title: Measuring Length in Grade 3: mm, cm, m and km (with Free Quiz)
meta_title: Measuring Length Grade 3: mm, cm, m, km
meta_desc: Teach measuring length Grade 3 mm cm m km the easy way: pick the right unit, master the conversions, and try a free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: The jump from Grade 2 is real: now a child meets millimetres and kilometres too, and has to convert between them. Here is how I teach the full mm-cm-m-km set so the conversions actually stick, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 3 child a ruler and ask how long their pencil is, and most will confidently say ‘12’ and stop there. Twelve what? That missing unit is the whole story of Grade 3 length. In Grade 2 a child measured in just centimetres and metres. Now the set widens to four: millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres. Measuring length in Grade 3 across mm, cm, m and km is really about two skills stacked together — choosing the sensible unit for a thing, and converting cleanly between units when the question forces you to.

I have taught this unit to eight-year-olds in Jaipur and Pune, and the same wall comes up every year: children can recite ‘1 metre is 100 centimetres’ and still write that a door is 2 centimetres tall. Knowing the fact is not the same as feeling the size. So I always start with size, not sums.

Which unit for which object

Before any conversion, a child needs a gut sense of how big each unit is. The quickest way is to tie every unit to something they can see in the room or on the way to school.

  • Millimetre (mm) — the thickness of a coin or an ID card. Tiny things: the width of a pencil lead, a grain of rice.
  • Centimetre (cm) — about the width of a fingernail. Everyday things: a crayon, a chapati’s thickness, a matchbox.
  • Metre (m) — roughly the height of a kitchen counter, or one big stride. Room-sized things: a door, a bed, a cricket pitch is 20 of them.
  • Kilometre (km) — a distance you walk in about 12 minutes. Journey-sized things: from home to the market, the length of a road.

My one rule of thumb for the class: if you would walk it, think kilometres; if you would lie down along it, think metres; if it fits on your desk, think centimetres; and if you can barely pinch it, think millimetres.

The conversions that matter in Grade 3

There are only three conversions a Grade 3 child truly needs, and each is a jump of ten, a hundred, or a thousand. Get these solid and everything else follows.

ConversionWhat it meansQuick check
1 cm = 10 mmTen little marks fill one centimetre on the ruler3 cm = 30 mm
1 m = 100 cmA metre stick has a hundred centimetre marks2 m = 200 cm
1 km = 1000 mA thousand metre strides make one kilometre5 km = 5000 m

Bigger to smaller: multiply

Going from a big unit to a small one, you multiply, because it takes many small units to fill one big one. To change 4 cm into millimetres, multiply by 10: 4 × 10 = 40 mm. To change 3 m into centimetres, multiply by 100: 300 cm. The number gets bigger, which feels right — you are counting in smaller pieces.

Smaller to bigger: divide

Going the other way, you divide. 250 cm into metres is 250 ÷ 100 = 2 m 50 cm. Here is the honest caveat I give every parent: Grade 3 children handle multiply-to-convert far more easily than divide-to-convert, so spend most of your practice time on the smaller-to-bigger direction. That is where marks are quietly lost.

Reading a ruler without slipping

The commonest measuring mistake at this age is not the unit at all — it is lining the object up with the 1 on the ruler instead of the 0. A pencil that reads ‘from 1 to 13’ is 12 cm long, not 13. Teach the habit out loud: ‘start at zero, read at the tip.’ For anything longer than the ruler, a measuring tape is the tool, and the same zero rule holds.

Between the big centimetre numbers sit the little millimetre marks — ten gaps in every centimetre. So a nail that ends three small marks past the 5 is 5 cm 3 mm, or 53 mm. Counting those tiny marks is genuinely good fine-motor practice, so I let children do it slowly at first.

Adding and subtracting lengths

Once units are steady, length turns into ordinary addition and subtraction — with one condition. You can only add or subtract lengths that share a unit. A ribbon 2 m 40 cm long with 60 cm cut off: convert to a single unit first, 240 cm − 60 cm = 180 cm, which is 1 m 80 cm. Line the units up like columns, the way you would with rupees and paise, and the arithmetic behaves.

ProblemSame-unit formAnswer
35 mm + 45 mm35 + 4580 mm = 8 cm
2 m 20 cm + 1 m 50 cm220 cm + 150 cm370 cm = 3 m 70 cm
5 km − 2 km 500 m5000 m − 2500 m2500 m = 2 km 500 m

A week that makes it stick

Ten focused minutes a day, and let the child measure real objects, not just fill boxes. Two days on choosing units (walk-lie-desk-pinch), two days on the three conversions, one day on ruler reading, and the weekend on mixed word problems where the child has to decide the unit and the operation. That deciding step is where fluency actually shows.

One counter-intuitive tip: hide the ruler sometimes. Ask a child to estimate the length of the table first, then measure. The gap between guess and reading is what builds real number sense for size — far more than another page of conversions ever will.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free 8-question quiz covering exactly this: choosing units, the mm-cm-m-km conversions, reading a ruler, and adding lengths. Let your child work through it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.about: Grade 3 measuring length: mm, cm, m, km and conversions

questions.q: Which unit best measures the length of a pencil?
questions.explanation: A pencil fits on your desk, so centimetres is the sensible unit — about 12 cm to 18 cm.

questions.q: How many millimetres are in 1 centimetre?
questions.explanation: There are 10 little marks in every centimetre, so 1 cm = 10 mm.

questions.q: How many metres are in 2 kilometres?
A pencil lies from the 0 mark to the 14 mark on a ruler. How long is it?
questions.explanation: Start at zero and read at the tip: from 0 to 14 is 14 cm.

questions.q: Which distance would you measure in kilometres?
questions.explanation: A journey you would walk is measured in kilometres; the others are small enough for mm, cm or m.
Both lengths share the unit mm, so add: 45 + 35 = 80 mm, which is also 8 cm.

questions.q: Convert 250 cm into metres and centimetres.
questions.explanation: Divide by 100: 250 ÷ 100 = 2 with 50 left over, so 250 cm = 2 m 50 cm.

faq.q: What length units does a Grade 3 child need to know?
faq.a: Four: millimetre (mm), centimetre (cm), metre (m) and kilometre (km). Grade 2 covers only cm and m, so mm and km — and converting between all of them — are the new Grade 3 skills.

faq.q: What are the length conversions to learn in Grade 3?
faq.a: Just three: 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 100 cm, and 1 km = 1000 m. To go from a bigger unit to a smaller one you multiply; from smaller to bigger you divide.

faq.q: How do I stop my child measuring from the wrong mark?
faq.a: Teach one habit out loud: start at zero, read at the tip. Lining an object up with the 1 instead of the 0 is the most common ruler error, and it makes every reading one unit too long.

faq.q: Can you add lengths that use different units?
faq.a: Not directly. Convert both lengths to the same unit first, add or subtract, then convert back if needed. For example, 2 m 20 cm + 150 cm becomes 220 cm + 150 cm = 370 cm, or 3 m 70 cm.
